Part E · Chapter 3

Cross-attention

How the words of a caption read the patches of a photo: the queries come from the text, the keys and values from the image

Cross-attention takes its queries from one sequence and its keys and values from another. The chapter works four patches by hand and studies BLIP, a captioning model, on four shark photos. On these photos, 17 to 27 empty patches take most of the weight at the last layer, and layer-averaged weights are a weak guide to which patches a word needs. Photos are credited under the figures.

You will need: queries, keys, values and the softmax (D4), the transformer block (D5), patches as tokens (E1) and encoders (E2).

Who asks and who answers

Guess first. In self-attention, a word's query (what it looks for), key (its label) and value (its content) all come from one text. A captioning model has read "a hammerhead shark with a tall" and is about to predict the next word. Which of the three would you make from the photo, and which from the words? Why?

In cross-attention the queries come from one sequence, the words being written, and the keys and values come from another, the photo's patches (squares of 16 × 16 pixels). Designers choose this because the word being written needs information that the patches provide. As in self-attention, a query is compared with the keys to give scores (dot products divided by a scale). A softmax turns the scores of one query into weights that add up to 1. The word receives the values multiplied by their weights and added together.

  1. Read the left table as self-attention within the caption written for this page, and the right table as cross-attention of the same words over the photo's 576 patches. A row is named after the word it writes, and its query is made from the word before it, because the model predicts a word from the words so far.
  2. Press Back twice, then Next step three times: queries, keys, weights and values appear in turn.

Sizes of the tables, for one head

The selected row

Photo: A scalloped hammerhead swimming in open blue water off Jarvis Island. Kevin Lino, NOAA/NMFS/PIFSC/ESD (NOAA Photo Library), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Weights: BLIP, mean of the 12 heads of the chosen decoder layer.

Both tables use one formula, with keys and values from the words (11 by 11, causal mask) or from the photo (11 by 577, no mask).

How it works

BLIP is a captioning model. Its decoder (the part that writes the caption) has 12 layers. A layer has 12 heads, copies of the attention computation with their own matrices of numbers. The photo has 24 × 24 = 576 patches. BLIP's vision encoder, which reads the photo, turns a patch into an image token, a vector of 768 numbers. It also adds one more token, the class token, so there are 577 tokens.

Count the weights for the 10-word caption. With the end token, a table has 11 rows, so for one head the cross table has 11 × 577 = 6,347 weights, one per word and token, and it has no mask. The causal mask hides the words after a word, so row r of the self table keeps r weights. In all, the self table keeps 1 + 2 + ... + 11 = 11 × 12 / 2 = 66 weights. In the equation below, KT is K with its rows and columns swapped, so an 11 × 64 table times a 64 × 577 table is an 11 × 577 table of weights. A head's query and key have 64 numbers (768 / 12).

one head:11 × 64output=softmax(Qqueries, 11 × 64, words×KTkeys, 64 × 577, photo÷ 8√64)×Vvalues, 577 × 64, photo

Common belief. A captioning model must put the photo and the words into one long sequence.

Why it fails. That is one design, the prefix design of the last section. In cross-attention the sequences stay apart: the 577 photo tokens are computed once, before the first word, so no information flows from the words into the photo.

Better account. The photo is a read-only source.

Quick quiz

A caption has 9 tokens and the photo 577. What size is one head's cross table, and how many entries does a mask remove?

It is 9 by 577, which is 5,193 weights. The cross part has no mask, so it removes none. The self part of the same layer has 9 by 9 entries and a causal mask that keeps 9 × 10 / 2 = 45.

In the equation, which of Q, K and V come from the photo, and how many rows do they have?

K and V come from the photo, and both have 577 rows, one for a token. Q comes from the words and has one row for a word.

Where the weights come from

The weights come from BLIP (Salesforce, BSD-3-Clause), run offline on four photos of the shark chapters. A model with cross-attention was needed, and the text decoder of BLIP is one. Both captions of a photo are run through BLIP's decoder word by word: BLIP's own, and one written for this page. Four photos is a small test, and the page says so where it matters.

Terms

target and source
the target is the sequence that supplies the queries (here the words) and the source is the sequence that supplies the keys and values (here the patches)
decoder
the part of a model that writes text, one token after another, with a causal mask (D5)
teacher forcing
feeding a model a text that is already known and reading what it computes at a position

Rows, layers and tokens

The query of a row is made from the vector of the word before it, as in D4, where the model predicts the next token from the last position. So the row "fin" is the query made from "tall", and it is used to write the word "fin". The first row is made from the start token and is used to write the first word. The "Next step" button goes through the four steps in turn, and "Play" does the same by itself, with a pause of 2.4 seconds between steps, until the last step.

A layer of BLIP's text decoder has three parts (D5): causal self-attention among the words, cross-attention to the photo, and an MLP. The figure shows the self part and the cross part of one layer together. A vision transformer (E1) cuts the photo into 24 by 24 patches of 16 by 16 pixels. The 577 tokens are computed once, before the first word, and all 12 layers of the decoder read the same 577 tokens with their own matrices \(W_K\) and \(W_V\). In the other design, shown by LLaVA in E4, the image tokens and the words form one sequence.

Symbols

\[ \mathrm{CrossAttn}(X_{\text{txt}}, X_{\text{img}}) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q_{\text{txt}}\,K_{\text{img}}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V_{\text{img}},\qquad Q_{\text{txt}} = X_{\text{txt}}W_Q,\quad K_{\text{img}} = X_{\text{img}}W_K,\quad V_{\text{img}} = X_{\text{img}}W_V \]

  • \(X_{\text{txt}}\) contains the vectors of the \(n_{\text{txt}}\) words (the stream of D5). \(X_{\text{img}}\) contains the \(n_{\text{img}}\) image tokens, 577 in BLIP, with 768 numbers apiece.
  • \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\) are learned matrices. They turn a vector of 768 numbers into a head's vector of \(d_k = 64\) numbers (12 heads of 64 give 768). \(\sqrt{d_k} = 8\).
  • The table of weights has \(n_{\text{txt}}\) rows and \(n_{\text{img}}\) columns, and a row sums to 1. For self-attention replace \(X_{\text{img}}\) by \(X_{\text{txt}}\) and apply the causal mask (D4).

The division by \(\sqrt{d_k} = 8\), where \(d_k = 64\) is the number of entries in a key, keeps the scores from growing with \(d_k\), as in self-attention.

Counting all heads and layers

The 12 heads give 6,347 × 12 = 76,164 cross weights per layer, and the 12 layers give 913,968. The self table has 66 × 12 = 792 allowed weights per layer, which is 9,504 for all heads and layers. The photo gets the larger table because it is the longer sequence, and the decoder reads it at all 12 layers.

Keys and values of the photo

The weights of cross-attention compare a vector built from words with a vector built from pixels. Training adjusts \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) so that the dot product of a word's query and a patch's key can serve as a score, as it does for two words in D4. A practical point: because the photo does not change while words are written, the keys and values of the photo can be computed once and kept. For BLIP that is 2 × 577 × 768 = 886,272 numbers per layer and 10.6 million for 12 layers, which is 21 MB at 16 bits. This is the same idea as the key-value cache of D5, applied to the source.

History

Cross-attention is older than the self-attention transformer. Bahdanau and others (2015) let a translation model search the source sentence for the words relevant to the next target word. The original transformer (Vaswani and others, 2017) kept it as the "encoder-decoder attention" layer. Xu and others (2015) used it to caption images, and showed the weights as maps over the photo. BLIP (Li and others, 2022) is a recent captioner built the same way.

In Python

import numpy as np
def cross_attention(X_txt, X_img, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    Q = X_txt @ Wq                        # n_txt x d_k
    K = X_img @ Wk                        # n_img x d_k
    V = X_img @ Wv                        # n_img x d_v
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[1])     # n_txt x n_img scores
    S = S - S.max(1, keepdims=True)       # for a stable softmax
    A = np.exp(S); A = A / A.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    return A, A @ V
rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)         # made-up numbers, d = 6, d_k = 4
X_txt = rng.normal(size=(3, 6))           # 3 words
X_img = rng.normal(size=(5, 6))           # 5 patches
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(6, 4)) / np.sqrt(6) for _ in range(3))
A, out = cross_attention(X_txt, X_img, Wq, Wk, Wv)
print(A.shape, out.shape)
print(A.sum(1).round(3))                  # a row adds up to 1
print(A.round(2))
(3, 5) (3, 4)
[1. 1. 1.]
[[0.07 0.08 0.02 0.06 0.77]
 [0.22 0.12 0.26 0.19 0.21]
 [0.16 0.34 0.2  0.24 0.06]]

The table has 3 rows (words) and 5 columns (patches). The output has the length of the text, 3, and the width of a value, 4. The patches are never changed. In this code the two lengths differ on purpose, so that a mistake in the transpose raises an error.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Test the sizes with different lengths for the two sequences. If both have 11 tokens, a transposed matrix still multiplies and the mistake goes unseen. Also check that the rows of the weights add up to 1 and that no mask was applied to the photo side.

More questions

Why can the keys and values of the photo be computed once?

They depend on the photo and on the matrices \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) alone. The words never change the photo tokens, so a new word needs one new query and no new keys or values.

Four patches by hand

Guess first. The word "fin" has the query (0.3, 1.5), and four patches have the made-up keys water (−1.2, 0.3), fin (0.2, 1.4), head (1.3, 0.4) and body (0.5, −1.1). Which patch gets the largest weight, and which the smallest? A dot product multiplies the matching numbers of two vectors and adds the results: (1, 2) and (3, 4) give 1 × 3 + 2 × 4 = 11. Work out the dot product of the query with one key first, so that you can see what makes a weight large.

As in the first section, the score of a patch is the dot product of the query and its key divided by √dk. Here dk = 2, because a key has two numbers. A softmax turns the four scores into weights that add up to 1, and the word receives the four values multiplied by their weights and added together.

  1. Look at the starting state: the coral arrow is the query and the navy arrows are the keys. A tile shows a patch with its dot product q·k and its weight.
  2. Under "A word's query" press "water", which sets the query to (−1.5, 0.3): the weights move to water 68%, fin 19%, body 8%, head 5%, and the output becomes (0.09, −0.46).
  3. Press "Shuffle the patches": the tiles change places, a tile keeps its weight, and the output is unchanged.

Keys of the four patches (navy) and the query (coral, drag its tip)

The four patches of the photo and their weights

Patches: four cells of the hammerhead photo (Kevin Lino, NOAA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons), squeezed as BLIP sees them. The keys and values are made up for this figure and are not from a trained model.

With the query of "fin" the weights are 57% (fin), 25% (head), 13% (water) and 4% (body), and the output is (−0.12, 0.49).

How it works

Take the query of "fin". The dot products with the keys of the fin, head, water and body are 2.16, 0.99, 0.09 and −1.50. For the fin, 0.3 × 0.2 + 1.5 × 1.4 = 2.16. Dividing by √2 = 1.41 gives the scores 1.53, 0.70, 0.06 and −1.06. Then es (e = 2.72) is 4.61, 2.01, 1.07 and 0.35, which add up to about 8.03, so the weights are 57%, 25%, 13% and 4%. The made-up values are fin (−0.7, 0.8), head (0.9, 0.7), water (0.2, −0.9) and body (0.6, −0.5). So the output is 0.57 × (−0.7, 0.8) + 0.25 × (0.9, 0.7) + 0.13 × (0.2, −0.9) + 0.04 × (0.6, −0.5) = (−0.12, 0.49).

\[ s_j = \frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}_j}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad a_j = \frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{4} e^{s_i}},\qquad \mathbf{o} = \sum_{j=1}^{4} a_j\,\mathbf{v}_j \]

Here q is the query, kj and vj are the key and the value of patch j, sj is its score, aj its weight and o the output. The exponential makes the weights positive, and the division by their sum makes them add up to 1. A sum does not depend on the order of its terms, so shuffling the patches leaves the output unchanged.

Common belief. The word "fin" looks for a fin patch and takes that patch.

Why it fails. The word receives a mix: the fin patch has 57% of the weight, and 43% goes to the other three patches.

Better account. The softmax makes a soft choice. A sharp choice needs a large gap between the scores, and the gaps depend on the queries and keys, which come from matrices that training adjusts.

Quick quiz

Make the query (0, 0). What are the weights, and why?

All dot products are 0, so the scores are 0 and e0 = 1 for the four patches. The softmax gives 25% to a patch, and the output is the plain average of the four values, (0.25, 0.025).

Does the output change if two patches swap places?

No. The score of a patch depends on the query and its own key, and the softmax adds the four scores in the same way in any order, so swapping places changes no weight. The output is a sum, and a sum has no order. For the model to use position, it must be added to the patch tokens before the keys are made.

Terms

score
the dot product of a query and a key, divided by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) (D4)
weight
the softmax of the scores of one query, so the weights of a word add up to 1
output
the weighted sum of the values, the new vector that the word receives

The dot product as a score

The dot product is large when the query and the key point the same way (0.5), so it works as a score.

A second case

A second case. Press "water", or drag the tip of the query to the left. The query (−1.5, 0.3) gives dot products 1.89, 0.12, −1.83 and −1.08. After the division by 1.41 the scores are 1.34, 0.08, −1.29 and −0.76. The exponentials are 3.81, 1.09, 0.27 and 0.47, which add up to about 5.63. The weights are 68% water, 19% fin, 8% body and 5% head. The query moved, and the weights followed it. The rest stayed fixed: the keys and values are fixed numbers, as they are when a trained model reads one photo.

Position

Cross-attention alone cannot tell where in the photo a patch lies, unless position is part of the keys and values. This is why a vision transformer adds position embeddings to its patch tokens (E1, which tested the effect by moving patches around).

Symbols

  • \(\mathbf{q}\) is the query of the word and \(\mathbf{k}_j\), \(\mathbf{v}_j\) are the key and the value of patch \(j\). Here \(d_k = 2\), so \(\sqrt{d_k} = 1.41\).
  • \(s_j\) is the score, \(a_j\) the weight and \(\mathbf{o}\) the output. This is the formula of the first section for one row and four columns.

Why it works, and where it misleads

The keys act like labels, the query like a request, and the values like the content that travels, and training adjusts the matrices that produce them. Here the labels have names ("fin") so that you can follow. In a trained model nobody names them, and a key is 64 numbers computed from a patch token. A weighted sum can also blur. If two patches get 50% apiece and their values differ a lot, the output looks like neither of them.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Switch off the division by \(\sqrt{2}\) and watch the weights become sharper: with the query of "fin" the fin patch rises from 57% to 68%. With 64 numbers per key the effect is larger (D4). If one weight is always near 100% from the first step of training, look at the scale before anything else. If all weights are about equal, the queries and keys are not yet useful.

Click a word, see the photo

Guess first. BLIP writes a caption one word at a time. For a word that names the animal, and for a background word such as "sand", which patches would you expect to get the most weight? Would layer 0, the first of the 12 decoder layers, already favour the animal?

A row of cross-attention has one weight per patch, so we can draw the row over the photo as a heat map. This is an attention map, and clicking a word shows the row that writes it. BLIP did not write this caption: it reads the words, and the row named after a word is the one that would write it. The animal is a region marked by hand (the dashed outline). We measure the share of a row's weight that falls inside it, so that we can compare it with the share of the patches that the animal covers.

  1. Start on the hammerhead photo at layer 11, the last layer, and click the words: about 25 of the same squares glow for all words. They are the empty patches of the next section.
  2. Tick "set the empty patches aside" and click "hammerhead": 52% of the weight falls inside the outline, which covers 22% of the patches. For "water" it is 10%.
  3. With the box still ticked, click layers 0, 3, 6, 9 and 11 for "hammerhead": the share inside rises from 19% to 25%, 28%, 36% and 52%.

About the captions and the marked outline

BLIP's own caption is its greedy output for the photo. The captions written for this page are passed through BLIP's decoder with teacher forcing, so BLIP did not write them. It gives several of their words a low probability. For "hammerhead" it is 0.02%, since BLIP would write "shark". The attention is what the decoder computes while it reads them. The animal outline is a rough polygon drawn by hand for this page. The photo is squeezed to 384 by 384 pixels before BLIP cuts it, and the grid is drawn back at the original proportions.

With the empty patches set aside, at layer 11 on the hammerhead photo, "hammerhead" puts 52% of its weight inside the animal (22% of the patches) and "water" puts 10%.

How it works

Take the row that writes "hammerhead" at layer 11. In the raw map, which counts all 576 patches, it puts 48.5% of its weight on the 27 empty patches and 27.0% inside the animal. Empty patches have image tokens that are almost zero, and the next section defines them. Setting them aside leaves 100% − 48.5% = 51.5% of the weight, so the share inside the animal is 27.0 / 51.5 = 52.4%.

share inside =27.0%weight inside the outline÷51.5%weight not on empty patches=52.4%shown as 52%

A row that spread its weight evenly would put about 22% inside the animal. So the row for "hammerhead" favours the animal, and the row for "water", with 10%, does not. An image token is computed from the whole photo, so a weight marks a place in the grid, and the pixels behind it may be elsewhere.

Common belief. A heat map shows what the model is looking at.

Why it fails. It shows where the weights of a row lie. The word receives the weighted sum of the values, so a patch with a short value adds little even with a large weight (the next section).

Better account. A heat map is a clue about where to look. To learn what the word used, test it (the section on hiding patches).

Quick quiz

The row for "water" puts 10% of its weight inside the animal, which covers 22% of the patches. Does the row favour the animal?

No. An even spread would put about 22% inside the animal, and 10% is less than half of that.

A row puts 40% of its weight on empty patches and 30% inside the animal. What is its share inside the animal when the empty patches are set aside?

The remaining weight is 100% − 40% = 60%, so the share is 30 / 60 = 50%.

The hammerhead photo, and layers

On the hammerhead photo at layer 11 the raw map of a word has the same bright squares for all words: 19 to 23 patches have at least half of the largest weight of the row, and all of them are among the 27 empty patches of the next section. With the empty patches set aside, "hammerhead" puts 52% of its weight inside the animal and "shark" puts 36%, and the animal covers 22% of the patches. "water" puts 10% there. At layer 0 the maps are flatter: for "hammerhead" the effective number of patches is 426 of the 549 patches that are not empty, against 310 at layer 11, and the share inside the animal is 19%, below the 22% of an even spread. From layer 0 to layer 11 that share rises (19%, 25%, 28%, 36% and 52% at layers 0, 3, 6, 9 and 11), and the page does not test why.

More cases

On the bamboo shark photo, with the empty patches set aside, the row that writes "shark" puts 69% of its weight inside the animal at layer 11. The animal covers 11% of the patches. The row that writes "sand" puts 5% there. Before the empty patches are set aside, the same patches glow for all words.

A second case, on the turtle photo. The row that writes "turtle" puts 40% of its weight inside the turtle (21% of the patches) and the row that writes "sand" 12%. On the white board photo the row of "shark" puts 38% inside the shark, which covers 9% of the patches, and the row of "ruler" 17%. These shares are for layer 11. At layers 0 and 3 the maps are flatter: for "turtle" the effective number of patches is 394 and 337 of 559, against 254 at layer 11.

What a row is preparing to write

A row is computed from the words before the word that it writes. Take the row that writes "pale" on the turtle photo, before the animal is named. It puts 62% of its weight inside the turtle (21% of the patches). A likely reason is that the next word names the animal, but the page does not test this. For small words the share inside the animal is close to or below the share of the patches that the animal covers: on the hammerhead photo "with" puts 21% and "in" 20% inside the animal (22% of the patches), and the end token puts 12%.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Before you read a heat map, read its scale. The readout gives the largest patch share and the effective number of patches. Take the row that writes "shark" at layer 11 on the bamboo shark photo, with the empty patches set aside. Its largest patch has 3% of the weight and the effective number of patches is 138 of 558, so the map is spread over many patches, and a bright spot is a slight preference. A map is drawn on its own scale, so a row with a largest weight of 4% looks as bright as one with 40%.

More questions

Why does the row of "a" at the start of the caption put more weight inside the animal than an even spread would?

On the hammerhead photo the row puts 44% there (22% of the patches). A likely reason is that the next word is about the animal and the row has no earlier words to go on, but the page does not test this.

The photo is squeezed to 384 by 384 before the 24 by 24 grid. How does that change what a patch is on the hammerhead photo?

A patch covers 16 by 16 pixels of the squeezed picture. In the original photo of 640 by 362 pixels it covers 26.7 pixels across and 15.1 down. A patch is wider than it is tall, and the figure draws the grid in the same way.

Where most of the weight goes

Guess first. In the raw maps of the last section, about 25 of the same patches glow for all words. What might those patches contain? And if a word puts 75% of its weight on them, how much of the photo does the word receive?

On these photos, 17 to 27 of the 576 patches are empty patches. Their image tokens are almost zero. The length of a vector is the square root of the sum of the squares of its numbers. These tokens have a length under 2, against a mean of 16 for the others (from 2.5 to 18). At the last layer the empty patches take 66% to 75% of the cross-attention weight (a mean over the 12 heads and the words of the page caption). A patch adds its weight times the length of its value vector, and what is added is the sum of these products over all patches. Their value vectors are short, so they supply only 3% to 6% of what is added.

  1. Look at the hammerhead photo at layer 11: the coral squares are the 27 empty patches (4.7% of the photo). The boxes under the plot give their weight and their share of what is added.
  2. Read the plot of all 12 layers on this photo: the navy line, the weight on the empty patches, stays between 69% and 90%. The dashed coral line, the share of what is added, stays between 5.5% and 16%. Drag the layer slider to read one layer.

The empty patches of this photo (coral)

By decoder layer, for all words of the page caption

Weights and lengths from BLIP. The photos are those of the figure above, credited there. An empty patch is a patch whose image token (the output of BLIP's vision encoder) is shorter than 2.

On the hammerhead photo 27 of the 576 patches (4.7%) take 74% of the weight at layer 11 and supply 5.5% of what is added.

How it works

Take the hammerhead photo at layer 11. The value vectors of the 27 empty patches have a mean length of 0.21, against 11.7 for the other patches. The weight on the empty patches, a mean over 12 heads and 11 rows, is 0.74 (the row for "hammerhead" alone has 0.485). Weight times length is then about 0.74 × 0.21 = 0.16 for them together and 0.26 × 11.7 = 3.0 for the others. So the empty patches supply 0.16 / (0.16 + 3.0) = 5% of what is added, and the figure, which works head by head, shows 5.5%.

for patch j:\(c_j = a_j\,\lVert\mathbf{v}_j\rVert\)what patch j adds (\(\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert\) is the length of \(\mathbf{v}\))|\(\dfrac{\sum_{j\in E} c_j}{\sum_{j} c_j}\)share added by the empty patches E

A softmax row must add up to 1, so the weight goes somewhere even when no patch matches the query.

Common belief. A weight of 75% on a patch means that 75% of the word's information comes from there.

Why it fails. A patch with a value of length 0.2 and a weight of 75% adds 0.75 × 0.2 = 0.15. A patch with a value of length 12 and a weight of 2% adds 0.02 × 12 = 0.24, which is more.

Better account. The weight says how the row divides its attention, and the length of the value says how much a part of it can add.

Quick quiz

A row has weight 0.8 on a patch whose value has length 0.2 and 0.1 on two patches with value length 12. What share of what is added comes from the first patch?

The three products are 0.16, 1.2 and 1.2, and they add up to 2.56. The first patch gives 0.16 / 2.56 = 6%, although it has 80% of the weight.

Why does the weight have to go somewhere when no patch matches the word?

A softmax row adds up to 1, so some patches must take the weight even when none matches. Where it goes depends on the scores, and in BLIP a large part of it goes to the empty patches.

Terms

empty patch
an image token of length under 2. The other 540 to 560 tokens of a photo have lengths from 2.5 to 18
value length
the length of a value vector, \(\lVert\mathbf{v}_j\rVert\); a short value adds little to a sum
share of what is added
the sum of weight times value length over the empty patches, divided by the same sum over all patches
attention sink
a token that takes weight without giving much back (D6)

Why the weight goes there

Why would a model do this? A softmax row must add up to 1 (D4). If no patch matches what the query wants, the weight still goes somewhere. One possible explanation, which this page does not test, is that the queries of the decoder give small or negative scores to most patches, so that the largest scores go to patches whose keys are nearly zero, since a dot product with a short key is near 0. The values of these patches are short too (0.21 against 11.7 on the hammerhead photo), so the weight that goes there adds almost no content to the word. The row is parked on a slot with no content. Some language models do this with the first token (D6), and in the left table of the first figure BLIP's start token takes 68% to 100% of the weight of a row at layer 11.

The numbers behind the claim

The numbers behind the claim, for the hammerhead photo. The empty patches have a mean token length of 0.86, against 15.6 for the others. At layer 11 the mean value length is 0.21 for them and 11.7 for the rest, a factor of 56. The weight on them, averaged over the 12 heads and the 11 rows of the page caption, is 74%. Multiply a weight by the length of its value, add up, and the empty patches supply 5.5% of the total. Compare 74% with 5.5%: a weight of three quarters adds one eighteenth of the total. Exercise 3 works a similar case. At layer 0 the weight share is 69% and the added share 7.2%. On the other photos at layer 11 the weight share is 68% (bamboo shark), 66% (white board) and 75% (turtle), and the added share 3.5%, 3.3% and 5.3%. Kobayashi and others (2020) argued for this correction in language models: look at the weight and at the length of the vector it multiplies.

How the empty patches were found

The rule is simple, and two routes agree. By length (under 2) it finds 27, 18, 22 and 17 patches on the four photos. By weight it finds the same patches on three photos and 21 of the 22 on the white board photo. The weight rule is a weight above three times the average of 1/576, taken over all words, heads and layers. The class token takes at most 0.4% of the weight of a row in the figures, and about 0.1% or less on average. On the four photos 83 of the 84 empty patches lie outside the hand-drawn outline of the animal. Darcet and others (2023) found high-norm artefact tokens in background regions of vision transformers, and added register tokens to give the model a place for them. Here the odd tokens are short, with a length under 2, so the mechanism may differ. That was not tested. Four photos is a small sample, so the rule describes these four photos only.

Symbols

  • \(a_j\) is the weight of patch \(j\) and \(\lVert\mathbf{v}_j\rVert\) the length of its value vector (0.5). The figure computes the sum per head, with the head's 64 numbers of the value, and averages over the rows.
  • This is a measure of how much a patch can change the word's vector. It does not say whether the change is useful, and the directions of the values can cancel.

In Python

import numpy as np
# one row over four patches; the last patch is an empty slot. Made-up numbers.
scores = np.array([-2.0, -1.5, -2.5, 0.0])       # the patches with content score below 0, the empty slot at 0
V = np.array([[1.0, 0.2], [0.8, -0.4], [0.1, 0.9], [0.0, 0.0]])
a = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum()
print("weights   ", a.round(2))
print("output    ", (a @ V).round(3))
b = a[:3] / a[:3].sum()                          # set the empty slot aside and renormalise
print("without it", (b @ V[:3]).round(3))
c = a * np.linalg.norm(V, axis=1)
print("added by the empty slot:", round(c[3] / c.sum(), 3))
weights    [0.09 0.15 0.06 0.69]
output     [0.224 0.008]
without it [0.731 0.027]
added by the empty slot: 0.0

Read the output. The empty slot takes 69% of the weight and adds no content: its share of what is added is 0.0. It still changes the result. The output with the slot is (0.224, 0.008), which is the output without it, (0.731, 0.027), times 0.31. The direction is the same and the length is 31% of the other. So the weight on an empty slot works like a volume knob: a row that puts 69% there has an output 31% as long as the output of a row that puts none there. This is why the figures offer "set the empty patches aside": the map then shows the direction of what the word receives, with the knob turned up to full.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Draw the maps of several different words side by side. A patch that is bright in all of them may be a sink: it takes weight whatever the word. Then check its value length. If it is short, set the patch aside and look at the rest, as the figures here do.

Twelve heads, one word

Guess first. A layer of BLIP's decoder has 12 heads, 12 copies of the cross-attention computation with their own matrices. The maps so far are means of the 12 heads. For the word "shark" at the last layer, would all 12 heads put most of their weight on the animal? If not, how would they differ?

The 12 heads of a layer can behave very differently, because a head has its own matrices for making queries, keys and values. No rule forces two heads to compute the same thing. In the figure one head puts most of its weight inside the animal and another puts most of its weight on the empty patches. The mean of the 12 maps mixes both.

  1. Keep "set the empty patches aside" ticked, choose the photos Hammerhead, Bamboo shark and Turtle in turn, and click the animal word of the photo ("hammerhead", "shark", "turtle"). The 12 small maps are the heads, numbered 0 to 11, and a label gives the head's share inside the animal and on the empty patches.
  2. Tick "sort the heads by weight inside the animal": head 9 comes first on all three, with 72%, 89% and 62%. On the hammerhead photo, the share of head 9 on the empty patches is 9%, against 93% for head 3.

At layer 11, head 9 puts 72%, 89% and 62% of its weight inside the animal on three photos, and the weakest head puts 8%, 11% and 6%.

How it works

Take "shark" on the bamboo shark photo, where the animal covers 11% of the patches. With the empty patches set aside, the 12 heads put between 11% (head 10) and 89% (head 9) of their weight inside the animal. Head 9 puts 7% of its weight on the empty patches and head 10 puts 82%, so the heads differ widely.

\[ \bar a_j = \frac{1}{12}\sum_{h=1}^{12} a_j^{(h)} \]

Here \(a_j^{(h)}\) is the weight that head \(h\) gives to patch \(j\), and \(\bar a_j\) is the weight shown in the maps of the earlier sections. A head counts for one twelfth of the mean, whatever it does. So a head that puts most of its weight on the empty patches counts as much as a head that points at the animal.

Common belief. The mean over the heads is the attention of the layer, and averaging loses no information.

Why it fails. Different sets of head maps can give the same mean, so the mean cannot tell which head put the weight where. A head that puts 90% of its weight on empty patches also adds a bright dot pattern to the mean.

Better account. Look at the heads one at a time first, then average with the empty patches set aside.

Quick quiz

Head 9 puts 89% of its weight inside the animal and the animal covers 11% of the patches. How many times more than an even spread is that?

The ratio is 89 / 11 = 8.1 times. An even spread would put 11% inside.

Why can the mean over the heads look less concentrated on the animal than the best head?

The mean adds the maps of heads with different behaviour. The sharp head is mixed with heads that spread out or park on empty patches, and it makes up one twelfth of the sum.

Terms

head
one of the 12 attention maps of a layer, with its own \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\) of 64 numbers apiece (D4)
specialisation
a head that behaves differently from its neighbours in a way that repeats over photos

Reading the heads

Click through the words and photos with "set the empty patches aside" ticked. Look for a head that is bright on the animal for the animal word and darker for a background word such as "sand". For the animal word, head 9 has the largest share inside the animal on the hammerhead, bamboo shark and turtle photos. On the white board photo, for "shark", head 7 has the largest share (60%) and head 9 has 38%. Tick the sort box to put the heads in order. Untick the other box to see how many heads park most of their weight on the empty patches. For "hammerhead" the share on the empty patches goes from 9% for head 9 to 93% for head 3. The mean over the heads mixes the two kinds, and about half of the weight of the mean map lies on the empty patches (49% for "hammerhead").

A second case

A second case. For the word "sand" on the bamboo shark photo, the heads put between 0% and 16% inside the animal, and the animal covers 11% of the patches. Heads do not all look at objects. For "ruler" on the white board photo, head 4 puts 49% inside the animal, and the animal is not what a ruler is. The ruler lies just below the shark, and the marked outline does not include it. Check the map before you trust the number, because a number inside a region you drew only tells you about that region.

Why the mean of the heads differs from the mean map

The box under the maps gives the mean of the 12 shares inside the animal: 53% for "shark" on the bamboo shark photo. The section on attention maps gave 69% for the same word and layer, because that figure shows the mean map. The share inside the animal of the mean map weights a head by the weight that it puts on the patches that are not empty: heads that park most of their weight on empty patches count little in it, and heads that point at the animal count more.

Why heads differ

Why heads differ: a head has its own matrices, and no rule forces two heads to learn the same thing. The loss only needs the sum of the outputs of the heads to be useful, so training can give different heads different jobs, and the maps above show heads that differ. Where it breaks: a head that looks specialised on four photos can be ordinary on others. This page shows head 9 on three photos, and it makes no claim about head 9 in general.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When a head-averaged map looks blurry, compute the spread of the 12 maps before you decide that the model is unsure. Twelve sharp maps that point to different places average to a blur.

Does the map show what matters?

Guess first. The row of cross-attention for the word "ruler" puts weight on some patches. In one trial you hide the 32 patches with the most weight, and in another 32 patches chosen at random. Which trial hides more of what the word needs, and would you expect the same for the word "hammerhead"?

To test whether an attention map shows which patches a word needs, we hide k patches. We paint them with the mean colour that BLIP subtracts from all photos (a grey). We then measure the fall: the drop in the log probability ln p, where p is the probability that BLIP gives to the word, in nats. A fall of 1 nat means that the word becomes e = 2.72 times less likely. If the weights point to the patches that matter, hiding the most attended patches, those with the most weight (the mean over the 12 layers), should lower the word more than hiding random ones.

  1. Start with "ruler" on the photo "Spadenose, white board", with the 32 patches of most weight hidden, and read the fall in the boxes: 4.97 nats.
  2. Choose "chance (random patches)": the fall, a mean of 20 random draws, is −0.07 nats.
  3. Choose the photo "Hammerhead, open water" with "attention, empty patches set aside", and set k to 128: the fall for "hammerhead" is −0.21 nats, so the word is not lowered. BLIP gives this word only 0.02% even with the whole photo, so little can be removed.

On the white board photo, hiding the 32 most attended patches (empty ones set aside) lowers "ruler" by 4.97 nats, and 32 random patches (mean of 20 draws) change it by −0.07.

How it works

Take "ruler" on the white board photo. BLIP gives it a log probability of −0.70, a probability of e−0.70 = 0.50. With the 32 attended patches hidden the log probability is −0.70 − 4.97 = −5.67, a probability of e−5.67 = 0.0035. So the word is e4.97 = 144 times less likely.

fall =\(\ln p_{\text{photo}}\)whole photo: −0.70−\(\ln p_{\text{hidden}}\)patches hidden: −5.67=4.97nats

The 40 words of the four captions (end tokens included) give 80 cases with k = 32 or 128, with the empty patches set aside. In only 6 of these cases did the fall from hiding the patches with the most weight (the mean over the 12 layers) exceed the fall from random patches by more than 0.3 nats. So in this test the weights, averaged over the layers, are a weak guide. A painted patch also makes a photo that BLIP never saw, and its response to that is part of what is measured.

Common belief. An attention map explains why the model wrote a word.

Why it fails. In this test the most attended patches lowered a word clearly more than random patches did in only 6 of 80 cases.

Better account. The map is a clue, and hiding patches tests the clue within the limits above.

Quick quiz

Hiding some patches lowers a word by 3 nats. By what factor is the word less likely?

By e3, which is about 20, because the fall is the logarithm of the ratio of the two probabilities.

On the hammerhead photo, the 128 most attended patches change "hammerhead" by −0.21 nats and 128 random patches (a mean of 20 draws) by −0.07. Do the attended patches matter more to the word?

No. Neither change lowers the word, so in this test the weights give no sign that these patches matter more to the word than random ones. BLIP also gives this word only 0.02% with the whole photo, so there is little to remove.

Terms

hiding a patch
setting its 16 by 16 pixels to the mean colour of BLIP's normalisation (the same numbers as CLIP's), which is 0 after normalisation
fall
the drop in the log probability that BLIP gives to the word, in nats (D3). A fall of 1 nat means the word became 2.7 times less likely
single-patch test
hide one patch at a time and record the fall of the word: 576 runs per photo. This is occlusion (B9)
rank correlation
how well two lists agree on the order of their items: 1 for the same order, 0 for no relation, −1 for the opposite order

More cases

Choose "ruler" on the white board photo, set the rule to attention with the empty patches set aside, and move k. At 32 patches (5.6% of the photo) the word's log probability falls by 5 nats, and about 19 of the 32 hidden patches lie on the ruler in the right-hand photo. Now choose "shark" on the same photo. The attention curve rises late, to 2.6 nats at 128 patches. The animal itself matters for this word: hiding all 51 animal patches lowers "shark" by 2.55 nats, and hiding 51 random background patches lowers it by 0.06. Now click through the other photos. For "hammerhead" on the hammerhead photo, hiding the 128 most attended patches changes the log probability by −0.21, while hiding 128 random patches changes it by −0.07: neither lowers the word. The single-patch test finds a fall of 0.57 with the same number of patches. Over the 40 words of the four photos, the median rank correlation between the attention of a row and the single-patch map is 0.02.

Three weak points of the test

The test has three weak points. First, hiding a patch with a grey patch makes a photo that BLIP never saw, and its response to that is part of what is measured. Second, a ViT patch token contains information from the whole photo after 12 blocks (E1). The weight points to a place in the token grid, and the pixels behind it may be elsewhere. Third, random hiding changes little: hiding 128 random patches (22% of the photo) changes the log probability by less than 0.5 nats for 39 of the 40 words. The single-patch rule costs 576 runs of the model, and it ranks patches one at a time. A group that matters only together can escape it. The ruler is the case. It is a long object, and hiding one patch of it changes little (0.37 nats for the best 32 patches). Attention points at the group, and hiding the group removes the ruler (4.97 nats).

What others found

This agrees with what Jain and Wallace (2019) found for language models: attention weights often disagree with other measures of importance. Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) replied that it depends on what one asks of an explanation, and that an attention map can be useful as one clue. Both are consistent with the figure. For "ruler" and "shark" on the white board photo the map is a clue at 128 patches, and for "hammerhead" the map gives no clue. For most words it falls short. The practical rule is to treat a map as a hypothesis. Test it with a deletion test or an occlusion map before you show it to a fisher as an explanation.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Run a deletion test on any explanation map: hide the patches that it ranks first, hide the same number at random, and compare the falls. If they match, the map gives no sign of what the word needed. Use the same number of patches for both.

More questions

For "ruler" the attention rule beats the single-patch test at 32 patches (4.97 against 0.37 nats). Why?

A likely reason is that the ruler is long. Hiding one of its patches leaves the rest visible, so one patch has a small effect and the single-patch test ranks them low, while the attention weights point at the whole ruler and hiding 32 of its patches together removes it. About 19 of the 32 hidden patches lie on the ruler.

Hiding the 51 animal patches lowers "shark" by 2.55 nats, and hiding 51 random background patches lowers it by 0.06. What does that say about the model?

For this word the model depends on the animal and not on scattered background patches. A good explanation of "shark" has to find the animal.

What the image costs

Guess first. A photo is cut into 576 patches and a caption has 12 words. About how many pairs of a query and a key does one head compute in a layer with cross-attention? About how many would it compute if the patches were placed in front of the words and read one another in both directions?

A pair is one query meeting one key and gives one weight, so counting pairs measures part of the cost of attention. A photo of side S pixels cut into patches of side P gives N = (S/P)2 image tokens. With cross-attention the photo adds nN pairs per head and layer of the decoder, where n is the number of words. In the prefix design the image tokens are placed in the sequence in front of the words. They read one another too, in both directions, which adds N2 pairs, and they pass through all the layers like words.

  1. Start with 384 pixels, patch side 16 and 12 words: the top two bars are pairs per head and layer, and the bottom two are multiply-adds per layer.
  2. Drag the photo side S to 768, or set the patch side P to 8: N becomes 2,304 and the pair ratio grows from 48.5 to 192.5.

Counts per head and per layer for a decoder of width 768 (BLIP's), as defined in the text. The multiply-adds count what the photo adds: the keys and values of the photo for cross-attention, and the whole block for tokens in the sequence.

At 384 pixels with 12 words, cross-attention computes 6,990 pairs per head and layer, and image tokens in the sequence need 338,766, which is 48.5 times as many.

How it works

Count the pairs for 576 image tokens and 12 words. In cross-attention the 12 words meet the 576 tokens, which gives 12 × 576 = 6,912 pairs. The words also read one another with the causal mask: word r meets r words, so the 12 words give 1 + 2 + ... + 12 = 12 × 13 / 2 = 78 pairs. The total is 6,990. In the prefix design the 576 tokens also read one another in both directions, which adds 576 × 576 = 331,776 pairs and gives 338,766 in all.

\[ N = \left(\frac{S}{P}\right)^{2},\qquad \text{pairs}_{\text{prefix}} = N^{2} + n\,N + \frac{n(n+1)}{2},\qquad \text{pairs}_{\text{cross}} = n\,N + \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \]

The term nN is the words reading the image tokens, and n(n + 1)/2 is the words reading earlier words. In the decoder, N2 exists only in the prefix design, because only there do the image tokens make queries. The vision encoder pays its own N2 in both designs. The multiply-adds, which count the multiplications and additions of a layer, give a smaller factor, 5.9 at these settings, and Go deeper shows the count.

Common belief. Cross-attention is cheaper, so it is the better design.

Why it fails. It is cheaper in pairs and multiply-adds, but it adds 28 million parameters to BLIP, and the words can read the photo only through the cross layers. The prefix design costs more per photo and needs no new layers.

Better account. The two designs spend different resources. The next chapter, on vision-language models, compares them.

Quick quiz

Halve the patch side from 16 to 8 on a 384 pixel photo. By what factor do the image tokens, the cross pairs and the prefix pairs change (12 words)?

The tokens go from 576 to 2,304, a factor of 4. The cross pairs go from 6,990 to 27,726 (about 4 times). The prefix pairs go from 338,766 to 5,336,142 (about 16 times), because the \(N^2\) term dominates.

Why does the prefix design have an \(N^2\) term while cross-attention does not?

In the prefix design the image tokens are tokens of the sequence, so all of them make queries that read the other image tokens. In cross-attention they are only keys and values, so they read none.

Go deeper multiply-adds, extra parameters, Python, debug tip about 3 min

Terms

image token
one patch turned into a vector (E1); \(N = (S/P)^2\) of them for a photo of side \(S\) and patch side \(P\)
pair
one query meeting one key; the number of pairs is the number of weights (D6)
prefix design
the image tokens are placed in front of the words and go through all layers of the language model like words (E4)

Multiply-adds

The multiply-adds tell the same story with a smaller factor. A block of width \(d\) spends about \(12 d^2\) multiply-adds per token on its attention matrices and its MLP (4 \(d^2\) and 8 \(d^2\), D5). In the prefix design the 576 image tokens spend that in a layer: 576 × 12 × 768² = 4.08 billion. In cross-attention the photo needs a key and a value per token (2 \(d^2\)), and a word needs a query and an output matrix (2 \(d^2\)). The total is (576 + 12) × 2 × 768² = 0.69 billion, a factor of 5.9. The count of pairs lets the image tokens read one another in both directions, as in a prefix that is not masked. A causal mask would halve the \(N^2\) term: 576 × 577 / 2 = 166,176 pairs instead of 331,776, and the ratio would be 173,166 / 6,990 = 24.8.

Extra parameters, and a narrow path

Two things complete the picture. First, cross-attention adds parameters. BLIP's decoder has 12 cross-attention sublayers of 2,363,904 numbers apiece, 28.4 million in total, which is 12.7% of the 224 million numbers of the model. The prefix design adds no layers and only a connection from the vision encoder (E4). Second, cross-attention lets the words read the photo only through those layers, so the path of the information is narrow, and a designer controls how wide it is. Flamingo (Alayrac and others, 2022) narrows it on purpose. It first reduces the photo to 64 tokens with a small resampler. In its 9 billion parameter model it adds cross-attention to one layer in four. This cuts the cost and the extra parameters, and the paper measures the loss of accuracy that follows.

Symbols

The count of pairs leaves out the class token, which would make \(N\) one larger. The number of words \(n\) is \(n_{\text{txt}}\) of the first section, and the word-to-word term \(n(n+1)/2\) is the causal triangle of D4. The size of a patch \(P\) is the one of E1.

In Python

def pairs_sequence(n_img, n_txt):          # photo in the sequence
    return n_img ** 2 + n_txt * n_img + n_txt * (n_txt + 1) // 2
def pairs_cross(n_img, n_txt):             # cross-attention
    return n_txt * n_img + n_txt * (n_txt + 1) // 2
for side in (224, 384, 768):
    n_img = (side // 16) ** 2
    s, c = pairs_sequence(n_img, 12), pairs_cross(n_img, 12)
    print(side, n_img, s, c, round(s / c, 1))
d = 768
print("multiply-adds per layer:", 576 * 12 * d * d, (576 + 12) * 2 * d * d)
224 196 40846 2430 16.8
384 576 338766 6990 48.5
768 2304 5336142 27726 192.5
multiply-adds per layer: 4076863488 693633024

Read the last row of the table. At 768 pixels the photo is 2,304 tokens. The prefix design needs 5.3 million pairs per head and layer, and the cross design needs 27,726. A language model with 32 layers and 32 heads multiplies both by 1,024. This is the reason why the long-context chapter (D6) matters for vision-language models, and why E4 measures the number of image tokens of actual models.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When a vision-language model runs out of memory on a large photo, count the image tokens first. Doubling the side of a photo multiplies the tokens by 4 and the prefix pairs by 16.

More questions

The keys and values of the photo are computed once. How many numbers does BLIP keep for them, for all 12 layers?

The count is 2 × 577 × 768 × 12 = 10,635,264 numbers, about 21 MB at 16 bits.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A decoder layer has 12 heads of \(d_k = 64\). A caption has 9 tokens and the photo has 577. Give the sizes of \(Q\), \(K\), \(V\) and the table of weights for one head. Give the number of weights for all heads of one layer. Give the number of numbers that must be kept so that the keys and values of the photo are not recomputed at a new word (12 layers).

    Hint

    The queries come from the words and the keys and values from the photo. Keep the keys and the values, for the heads of all layers.

  2. theory Show that the output of cross-attention does not change if the \(n_{\text{img}}\) patches are put in a different order. Then say what must be added to the patch tokens so that the model can tell where a patch was, and where in this primer that was done.

  3. theory A row of weights is (0.80, 0.10, 0.10) over three patches, with value lengths (0.2, 12, 12). Find the share of the weight and the share of what is added for the three patches. Then find the length of the output when the first patch is set aside and the row is renormalised, if the three values are parallel with the stated lengths.

    Hint

    The share of what is added of patch \(j\) is \(a_j \lVert v_j\rVert\) divided by the sum over the three patches.

  4. theory The self part of a decoder layer has a causal mask and the cross part has none. Explain why the two choices are made. What would go wrong if the cross part had a mask that hid the right half of the photo from all words?

Practice

  1. practice Write cross_attention as in the first code block with \(d_k = 4\) and your own seed. Check that the rows add up to 1. Replace one patch's key and its value by the zero vector. Report the weight it receives, and the change of the output when you set it aside and renormalise.

  2. practice Open data/blip.json of this chapter (https://mailab.in/primer/e3-cross-attention/data/blip.json) with Python. For the set bamboo-1-page, read the field read at layer index 4 (layer 11). The entry at index 3 (counting from 0) is the share of the weight inside the animal with the empty patches set aside. Divide it by the share of the animal in patches (66 of 576) and list the words with a ratio above 3.

  3. practice Extend pairs_sequence and pairs_cross to count pairs for all 12 heads and 12 layers. Plot the ratio of the two against the patch side \(P\) from 8 to 64, for a photo of side 384 and 12 words. Say where the ratio is largest.

Think deeper

  1. open BLIP writes "shark" for the hammerhead photo and gives "hammerhead" a probability of 0.02%. SharkCam wants the species. Where could the missing knowledge be: in the image tokens, in the cross-attention, or in the language side? Design a test for the three, say which photos and which measurement you would use, and what result would exclude a place.

  2. open You want to show a fisher a map that explains why SharkCam flagged a frame. Which of the methods in this chapter and in B9 would you offer? How would you check that the map is faithful for that frame? What would you write under the map?

  3. open A new captioning model might park weight on empty tokens too. Design a check that finds such tokens from the model's own numbers, without a human marking the animal. Say which two measurements you would combine and what false findings you expect.

Come back later

Answer after two days and again after a week, without looking back.

Write cross-attention in one line. Say which of Q, K and V come from the photo. Say what differs from self-attention in the size of the table of weights.

softmax(Q_txt K_img^T / sqrt(d_k)) V_img. K and V come from the photo and Q from the words. The table has the words as rows and the patches as columns, with no causal mask. The table of self-attention is square and triangular (sources).

D4 showed that a causal model needs a mask or it leaks the answer. Why does cross-attention to a photo not need one?

The photo is not part of the text that is being predicted. Reading all of it, before and after, leaks no information about the next word. The words still need the mask in the self part (D4).

B9 showed an occlusion map for a CNN. How does the occlusion test of this chapter relate to the attention map, and which one would you trust to say what a word needed?

Occlusion measures the effect of hiding patches on the model's own output, and the attention map only reports weights. For what the word needed, trust the occlusion test, and use attention as a clue (occ, B9).

  4. Xu, K., Ba, J., Kiros, R., Cho, K., Courville, A., Salakhutdinov, R., Zemel, R., Bengio, Y. (2015). Show, attend and tell: neural image caption generation with visual attention. ICML 2015. arXiv:1502.03044. Attention maps over a photo while a caption word is written.
  5. Darcet, T., Oquab, M., Mairal, J., Bojanowski, P. (2023). Vision transformers need registers. ICLR 2024. arXiv:2309.16588. High-norm artefact tokens in background regions, and register tokens.
  6. Kobayashi, G., Kuribayashi, T., Yokoi, S., Inui, K. (2020). Attention is not only a weight: analyzing transformers with vector norms. EMNLP 2020. arXiv:2004.10102. Weights and the lengths of the vectors they mix.
  7. Jain, S., Wallace, B. C. (2019). Attention is not explanation. NAACL 2019, arXiv:1902.10186. Wiegreffe, S., Pinter, Y. (2019). Attention is not not explanation. EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, arXiv:1908.04626. The two sides of the debate on attention as explanation.
  8. Alayrac, J.-B., and others (2022). Flamingo: a visual language model for few-shot learning. NeurIPS 2022. arXiv:2204.14198. Cross-attention layers inserted into a frozen language model (one layer in four for the 9B model), 64 visual tokens per image.
  9. Dosovitskiy, A., and others (2021). An image is worth 16x16 words. ICLR 2021. arXiv:2010.11929. The vision transformer of E1, which is BLIP's image encoder.
  10. Photos: Wikimedia Commons, credited under the figures (data/sharks/photos.json). The animal outlines are drawn by hand for this page. The data were computed by data/make_blip.py and data/make_occlusion.py: 8 captions on 4 photos, 576 single-patch runs per photo and rule tests with 20 random draws per size. The empty patches are those with an image token of length under 2. The rank correlation is over the patches that are not empty.
